extracted.intended_audience: authors, referees, and journal editors (molecular/cell biology)
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial policy and practical standards for transparent, fair, and efficient peer review at a selective scientific journal (The EMBO Journal), covering selection criteria, scooping protection, publication of review files, cross-referee commenting, manuscript transfer, and co-refereeing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish editorial-process efficiency metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: A unique feature of The EMBO Journal is that we publish data on the efficiency of the editorial process (e.g. acceptance rates, decision times, rounds of revision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish submission, revision and decision times (dates are not reset upon resubmission following substantial revision). Provide statistics such as percent accepted, average time to editorial and post-review decisions, fraction rejected before formal peer review, and other 'vital statistics' to demonstrate speed and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-cut selection criteria (high 'first cut')
rubrics_metrics.description: Only manuscripts that fit within the journal's scope, that present a sufficiently striking advance and that have a real chance of being published with realistic further revision continue to the more time-intensive peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an initial editorial screen to reject papers early when they do not meet scope/impact/realistic publishability thresholds (EMBO: 74% rejected before formal peer review). Employ editorial advisory board input where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid raising new issues in revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that no new issues are raised that were not brought forward in the initial review (excluding points on data added in revision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit reviewer/editor requests during revision to issues already identified in initial review to prevent scope creep and unnecessary extra work for authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scooping protection policy
rubrics_metrics.description: A study will not be rejected on account of having been scooped while it is under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional experimentation is required, specify when to expect a revision (usually around 3 months). During this period the author is immune from rejection due to scooping provided related publications are immediately discussed with the editor. If a revision will take longer and no related literature has appeared, the deadline can usually be extended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for broad, deep studies over 'salami slices' and rejection of derivative work
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative work will not be accepted in a highly selective journal; the journal wants to encourage broad and deep studies over 'salami slices'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage premature, minimal-publishable-unit submissions and prioritize comprehensive mechanistic or physiologically significant studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish peer review process files (referee reports, author responses, decision letters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority of papers are accompanied by a detailed document presenting the referee comments, author responses and editorial decision letters of every round of review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit files only for typos; keep them optional (authors may opt out at any stage). Inform referees that their reports may be published upon acceptance. Be prepared to remove sensitive data from files if authors have good reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention and transparency of timestamps
rubrics_metrics.description: The actual submission, revision and decision times are published; dates are not reset upon resubmission following substantial revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide transparent timelines for the review/decision lifecycle to allow accountability on speed and process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use process files for education and credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review process files can serve as educational tools and as a way to acknowledge referees' contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showcase reports to demonstrate that refereeing is constructive and to teach peer review practices; consider ways to provide tangible credit for anonymous referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript transfer and referee-report recycling
rubrics_metrics.description: Support author-controlled manuscript transfer between journals (the four EMBO titles) including transfer of peer review reports and identities to avoid repeated refereeing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should recommend transfer for scope reasons and may discuss manuscripts across journals to pre-programme a successful outcome. Encourage reuse of high-quality referee reports to reduce reviewer burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage cross-referee commenting (post-review feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Send the reports to all referees a day before the decision and actively encourage feedback so referees can comment on each other's reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect every referee to comment; post-review feedback is especially useful to correct erroneous/non-essential issues, note perceived bias, or reinforce overlooked essential points. This step should not delay the editorial decision (decision made with or without additional feedback).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate routine 'confidential comments' box (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of transparency, the journal has dropped the 'confidential comments' box from referee reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain confidential-direct-to-editor communication only for rare cases (ethical concerns, data integrity, biosecurity, undeclared conflicts of interest) which should be communicated directly to the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-refereeing (mentored reviewing) policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal allows co-refereeing with one other senior member of a referee's laboratory as part of the mentoring process only if the primary referee has independently evaluated the manuscript and agrees with the report filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict of interest and confidentiality rules apply to both referees. For accountability and appropriate credit, request that the name of the co-referee be documented to the editors. Reserve co-refereeing for experienced postdocs and ensure the primary referee's independent assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial arbitration and disambiguation of reviewer input
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional editors read referee reports and author responses impartially to publish the best papers possible and to disambiguate essential criticisms from further-reaching suggestions based on personal preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize editors are generalists who should weigh well-argued referee reports heavily but must separate essential methodological/interpretive issues from subjective preferences when making decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and report outcome indicators to validate process robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: Use outcome metrics (e.g. fraction of papers published after invited revision, subsequent publication trajectory of rejected manuscripts, appeals rate) to assess the editorial process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite indicators such as '97% of cases where a revision is invited are published' and 'appeals rate 6.4%' as evidence of selection correctness and editorial robustness; monitor where rejected manuscripts are later published to check for mistaken rejections.
